specPoints.text: know that the stopping distance of a vehicle is made up of the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance
describe the factors affecting vehicle stopping distance, including speed, mass, road condition and reaction time

primer.text: An emergency stop happens in two acts: the driver's reaction, then the brakes' work. Each act consumes road, and their sum decides whether the vehicle stops in time. This note splits the total into its two distances, then lists the factors that stretch either half.

lessons.title: Thinking distance and braking distance
lessons.opening: From hazard to halt, the car covers two distances for two reasons. First the driver reacts — the thinking distance; then the brakes bite — the braking distance. The stopping distance is their sum, and the highway data shows how steeply that sum climbs with speed.
keyPoints: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
Thinking distance is the distance travelled while the driver reacts to the hazard and prepares to stop.
The average human reaction time is about 0.25 s, and it lengthens with tiredness, distractions, alcohol or drugs.
Braking distance is the distance travelled under the braking force.
For a given braking force, the greater the speed, the greater the stopping distance.

low.restatement: One part of the stop happens before the brakes even bite (thinking), the rest while they bite (braking); add them for the stopping distance.
low.analogy: A relay race: the reaction leg and the braking leg. The race's length is the two legs added, never either alone.
low.examPointer: Quote the formula in words first — 'stopping = thinking + braking' — then substitute numbers.

medium.restatement: The thinking distance is speed × reaction time, so it scales with both; the braking distance grows even faster with speed, which is why the highway-code table's column more than triples from 20 to 60 mph.
medium.analogy: Thinking distance is how far a dropped ball falls during your blink; braking distance is how long the brakes need — both stretch when the pace rises.
medium.examPointer: A 'calculate the braking distance' question is a rearrangement: braking = stopping − thinking. Subtract in the right order.

check.stem: The stopping distance of a vehicle is the sum of:

options.explanation: Those are not distances.
This is the sum law of record.
Those are factors, not the two distances.
Only one braking leg exists.

check.stem: Thinking distance is the distance travelled while the driver:

options.text: Applies the brakes at maximum force
options.explanation: That is the braking leg.
No acceleration happens in an emergency stop.
Gear changes play no part.

options.text: Reacts to the emergency and prepares to stop
options.explanation: The reaction window is exactly what the thinking distance covers.

check.stem: The average human reaction time of record is:

options.explanation: Far shorter than the quoted figure.
Far longer than the quoted figure.
About a quarter of a second.
Ten times too long.

check.stem: Which condition lengthens a driver's reaction time?

options.text: Tiredness, phone distraction, alcohol or drugs
options.explanation: All four raise the reaction time, stretching the thinking distance.
Those do not lengthen the reaction.
Engine noise is not the listed driver.
Lighting is not a reaction-time factor of record.

check.stem: The braking distance is the distance covered:

options.explanation: That is the thinking leg.

options.text: Under the braking force, in metres
options.explanation: The braking leg's definition of record.
No distance is covered after stopping.
An emergency stop decelerates.

check.modelAnswer: It is the stretch of road consumed while the braking force acts on the vehicle, measured in metres.

check.stem: Define reaction time and quote its average value.
check.modelAnswer: Reaction time is the interval between seeing a hazard and reacting to it; the human average is about 0.25 s.

check.stem: Explain why a driver's thinking distance grows with speed even at a fixed reaction time.
check.modelAnswer: Thinking distance is the speed multiplied by the reaction time. With the reaction time fixed, a faster vehicle covers more ground during that same pause, so the thinking distance rises in direct proportion to the speed.

check.stem: At 20 m/s a vehicle stops in a total of 40 m, having covered 14 m during the driver's reaction. Calculate the braking distance.
check.modelAnswer: Braking distance = stopping distance − thinking distance = 40 − 14 = 26 m.

lessons.title: Speed and the other stopping factors
lessons.opening: The sum law tells you how the stop is built; the factor list tells you when it balloons. Speed leads the list — the highway data puts the 60 mph stop at six times the 20 mph stop — and mass, road condition and reaction time complete it.
keyPoints: Vehicle speed: greater speed means a greater braking distance, since the brakes must do more work.
Vehicle mass: the more massive the vehicle, the further it travels while stopping.
Road condition: wet or icy roads make the brakes less effective and lengthen the stop.
Driver reaction time: distraction, tiredness, medication, alcohol or drugs all stretch the thinking distance.
The Highway-Code table of record runs from 12 m at 20 mph to 73 m at 60 mph.

low.restatement: Four levers stretch the stop: go faster, carry more, lose grip, react slower.
low.analogy: Filling a bath faster: wider tap (speed), deeper tub (mass), blocked drain (road), late start (reaction) — all four raise the flood line.
low.examPointer: Factor questions want all four of record — listing two scores partially.

medium.restatement: The four factors divide by leg: reaction time stretches the thinking distance; speed, mass and road condition stretch the braking distance — speed worst of all, as the table's steep climb shows.
medium.analogy: Two taps feed one pool: the reaction tap and the braking tap. Speed, mass and grip feed one; the phone in the driver's hand feeds the other.
medium.examPointer: When asked 'why is the stopping distance so much larger at 60 mph', cite the table values (12 m to 73 m) — evidence beats assertion.

check.stem: Which factor list affects vehicle stopping distance?

options.text: Speed, mass, road condition, reaction time
options.explanation: The four of record.
Colour is irrelevant.
Speed and road condition belong too.

options.text: Engine size, tyre brand, music volume
options.explanation: None of those is on the list of record.

check.stem: For a fixed braking force, increasing the vehicle's speed makes the stopping distance:

options.text: Shorter, because less stopping is needed
options.explanation: Faster travel means more stopping to do.

options.text: Unchanged, since the brakes are the same
options.explanation: The brakes being unchanged does not freeze the distance.
The greater the speed, the larger the stopping distance.
No speed yields a free stop.

check.stem: A fully laden lorry needs a longer stop than the same lorry empty, at the same speed, chiefly because:

options.text: Its driver reacts more slowly when loaded
options.explanation: Loading does not touch the driver's reaction.

options.text: The greater mass travels further while stopping
options.explanation: Mass is a listed factor: more massive, more distance.

options.text: The road becomes icier under load
options.explanation: Loading does not change the weather.
Nonsense; the brakes remain.

check.stem: Which change stretches the braking distance rather than the thinking distance?

options.explanation: That feeds the reaction leg.
Grip loss feeds the braking leg.
That feeds the reaction leg.
Reaction again.

check.stem: The table shows 20 mph stopping at 12 m and 60 mph at 73 m. The comparison proves that stopping distance grows:

options.text: In fixed steps of 12 m per 20 mph
options.explanation: The steps widen: 23, 36, 53, 73.
The table contradicts that outright.

options.text: Steeper than proportionally with speed — over sixfold for a threefold speed rise
options.explanation: 60/20 is a threefold speed rise; 73/12 is a sixfold distance rise.
Sixfold for threefold is not exact proportion.

check.stem: List the four factors of record for vehicle stopping distance.
check.modelAnswer: Vehicle speed, vehicle mass, road condition and driver reaction time.

check.stem: State what happens to the braking distance when speed increases at a fixed braking force.
check.modelAnswer: It increases: the greater the speed, the greater the stopping distance.

check.stem: Explain why icy roads lengthen a vehicle's stopping distance.
check.modelAnswer: Ice reduces the grip between tyres and road, so the brakes work less effectively. With the braking force less effective, the vehicle travels further while coming to a stop — the braking distance stretches.

check.stem: A lorry's thinking distance is 15 m and its braking distance is 38 m. Calculate its stopping distance.

glossary.definition: The total distance a vehicle travels during an emergency stop: thinking distance plus braking distance.
The distance travelled while the driver reacts to the hazard and prepares to stop.
The distance travelled under the braking force.
The interval between seeing a hazard and reacting to it; about 0.25 s on average.

workedExample.prompt: At a speed of 20 m/s a vehicle's total stopping distance is 40 m, and it covers 14 m while the driver reacts. Calculate the braking distance.
steps: Identify the variables: stopping distance = 40 m, thinking distance = 14 m.
Rearrange the sum law: braking distance = stopping distance − thinking distance.
